Y. 13901, U.S.A. Received 19 September 1972 Revised version received 1 December 1972 The paleomagnetism of the Late Cretaceous Polos de Caldas alkaline complex (46.6°W, 21.9°S) was investigated through 42 oriented cores from seven sites. Six sites, reversed relative to the present magnetic field of the Earth, yield a pole at 127°W, 82°S (dp= 8 °, dm= 13°). This pole is located close to other Late Cretaceous poles for South America obtained by Creer [1] from untreated paleomagnetic samples. The results are significantly different from those for the nearby Early Cretaceous Serra Geral basalt but close to the Triassic pole for South America. The polar wandering path for South America for the Mesozoic seems to be more complicated than anticipated. The available paleomagnetic information may not yet be precise enough to determine the time of opening of the Atlantic. 1. In

wandering path for South America for the Mesozoic seems to be more complicated than anticipated. The available paleomagnetic information may not yet be precise enough to determine the time of opening of the Atlantic. 1. Introduction Paleomagnetism of Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks of South America and Africa probably records the opening of the South Atlantic. Unless such opening was through a rotation about a pole close to the axis of rotation of the Earth, the time of this tectonic phenomenon should be recorded by a fork in the superimposed polar wandering curves of South America and Africa. This report presents new paleomagnetic information on the Late Cretaceous of South America and evaluates it in relation to other available data. Oriented cores were taken with the assistance of I. Pacca of the Institute of Physics of the University of S5o Paulo. Paleomag- netic laboratory measurements were done at Lamont- Doherty Geological Observatory of Columbia University. 2. (U.S.A.] Received September 16, 1974 Revised version received November 14, 1974 A Paleocene granodiorite pluton on Jamaica has been subject to extensive weathering caused by the tropical marine environment of the island. The natural remanence of 29 samples obtained from relatively fresh rock in two localities was found to consist of two components with overlapping coercivity ranges. Alternating field treatment proved ineffective for removing the secondary component without destroying the primary one. Thermal demagneti- zation of samples from the two localities was more effective and yielded paleomagnetic poles at 14.7 ° N, 11.6°W and 58.9 ° N, 15.9°E respectively. These pole positions are different from those available from contemporaneous North American rocks and from poles derived from Jamaican Cretaceous and Upper Miocene rocks. Mineralogical studies showed that the granodiorite has undergone an extensive maghemitization superposed on earlier class 2 deuteric oxidation and related to the weathering p

different from those available from contemporaneous North American rocks and from poles derived from Jamaican Cretaceous and Upper Miocene rocks. Mineralogical studies showed that the granodiorite has undergone an extensive maghemitization superposed on earlier class 2 deuteric oxidation and related to the weathering process. Some of the titanomaghemite has, however, been converted to titanohematite. Hence although the secondary remanence carried by the former was removable by thermal treat- ment at 500°C, its part carried by the latter could not be removed without simultaneously destroying the primary remanence carried by the residual titanomagnetite. The observed paleopole positions do not, therefore, represent the true Paleocene geomagnetic field, but suggest that the direction of magnetization of the pluton has been approx- imately equatorial and was probably acquired in a reversed geomagnetic field. This could be interpreted as having been caused by the behavior of the geomagnetic field during a polarity transition, but a more favorable interpretation appears to be a large anticlockwise tectonic rotation of the islands since the Paleocene. 1. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: in-section studies using transmitted light. An abundance of decomposed or partly decomposed ferromagnesian minerals was observed. Turner [ 11 ] has described a natural process whereby the decomposition products of ferromagnesian minerals eventually break down into magnetite when heated in an oxidizing atmosphere. It would appear that in the present case a similar effect has taken place in the laboratory and that heat treatment has "generated" some magnetite from the decomposition products of the ferromagnesian minerals already present in the rocks. This was suggested by the results of experiments summarized in Fig. 2 which shows thermomagnetic curves and curves describing imposi- tion of isothermal remanence. Magnetic material ex- tracted from the granodiorite underwent a decrease in saturation magnetization after cooling from the Curie temperature (Fig. 2a). This was evidently caused by oxidation of magnetite to hematite. It was emplaced in the Early Tertiary as a solid intrusion, but probably was above its Curie temperature at the time and so became magnetized substantially in situ. If so, it must have undergone considerable tectonic disturbance subsequent to emplacement and magnetization, including an important component of clockwise rotation. Examination of paleomagnetic data for the westernmost Cordillera shows that an abnormal number of rock bodies have discordant directions of remanent magnetization, mostly clockwise rotations of declina- tion, flattened inclinations, or both. Introduction St. Paul and Amsterdam (Fig. 1), the only parts of the mid-Indian ridge axis which are above sea level, are amongst the world's most isolated islands, thus provid- ing the only simple means to observe geological prop- erties in a large region. Methods Field. Up to eight separate cores of 2.5 cm diame- ter and average length 12 cm were drilled from each of 15 separate lava and 3 minor intrusive bodies on the island, using a gasoline-powered portable drill. Spacing between cores in each body averaged 5 m. Samples were oriented in geographic coordinates to a precision of-+2.5 ° while still attached to outcrop. The locations of the sample sites are given in Fig. 2. Laboratory. Directions of remanent magnetism be- fore and after treatment in peak alternating magnetic fields of 100 and 200 oersteds were measured using a spinner magnetometer. Samples were selected for K/At dating using two criteria: the bodies involved should be in known strati- graphic sequence, and the samples should be fresh and unaltered. The sedimentary episode during which the Embalse Rio Tercero Formation was formed, was interrupted by a volcanic cycle. During this cycle more than seven lava flows were formed; sediments which were laid down between the lava flows have the same charac- teristics as those formed before the volcanic cycle [6]. The Vulcanitas Cerro Colorado Formation include the lava flows extruded in this first volcanic cycle and their interbedded continental sediments. Rocks of this formation are fairly well exposed in the Cerro Colo- rado area, about 32 ° South, 64 ° West. The petrographic characteristics of the volcanic rocks of the Sierra de los Cdndores Group are de- scribed by Gordillo and Lencinas [6]. According to these authors six lava flows and one diabasic dyke are exposed at the Cerro Colorado area. Mentioned in chronological order, and according to the petrographic study, the lava flows are: (1) Picrite basalt; (2) Calc- alkalic trachyte, lower flow; (3) Black-trachybasalt lower flow; (4) Calc-alkalic trachyt, upper flow; (5) Brown-trachybasalt, and (6) Black-trachybasalt, upper flow, fig. 1. Introduction Palaeomagnetic results from the Miocene to recent volcanics of the East African rift system have been re- ported by several authors [1-3]. The pole position for the Ethiopian flood basalts [4] considered to be Eocene-Oligocene in age shows a 9 ° deviation from the present pole as compared to the small 5 ° de- viation of the Miocene pole. The next oldest known pole for Africa is the one obtained from the Lupata series volcanics [5] with an age of" 110 my [6]. For the period 200 my- 110 my, eight other poles are available and because of their close grouping, Briden [7] concluded that the African continent was sta- tionary during this period. The mean of

ge are lacking because of the unavailability of such rocks in East Africa. The result obtained from the alkaline com- plexes of Tororo and presented here helps to fiU a gap in the polar wander path for Africa. 2. Geology and age The alkaline complexes of S.E. Uganda lie on a line * Now with Canadmn Universities Service Overseas (CUSO), Ottawa, Canada. which runs a little east of north from Sukulu through Tororo, Bukusu, Sekululu to Budeda. They are broadly similar, with a central carbonatite core surrounded by a ring of syenite and ijolite. Carbonatite forms the main mass of the prominent outcrops at Tororo hill, from where the samples were collected. No radiometric date is available for these forma- tions. An alternative explanation of the Lower Palaeozoic European palaeomagnetic results is that favoured by Briden [17] which involves an ex- cursion of the pole from a quasi-static position in the mid-Ordovician to mid-Silurian, and return to its for- mer position in the mid-Silurian to early Devonian, combined with some remagnetization of European Lower Palaeozoic results. I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. So after the Silurian Period the south palaeo- magnetic pole returned eastwards passing close to its Cambrian and Ordovician positions. This preferred explanation, of course, implies that remagnetization has not been as extensive as envisaged by Creer. North American Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results are scarce and a sensible polar wander path is difficult to construct. Creer again champions an ex- planation of the results in terms of remagnetization. This interpretation has been debated in the literature

d agreement with the geo- logical ideas outlined above on the age and origin of the Hercynian and Uralian mountain chains. The polar wander paths of the blocks associated with these oro- genies can be seen to converge by the Carboniferous. The separation of land masses across the ocean now represented by the Hercynian and Appalachian moun- tain belts was about 60 ° of arc (greater than the size of the present Atlantic) in the Cambrian Period. The palaeomagnetic results, however, do not fit in with the geological knowledge of the history of the Caledonian mountain chain [21 ]. The most noticeable problems are that (i) there is no hairpin bend in the North Ameri- can record, corresponding to that in the European and (ii) the Ordovician and Cambrian pole positions for the two blocks lie very close to each other. Neither of these suggests the "proto Atlantic" closed during the Silurian to form the Caledonian mountain chain. Further Lower Palaeozoic results from North America are needed before these apparent contradictions can be explained. Acknowledgements I wish to thank Professor K.M. Introduction Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic collections from South America were made in 1956 and 1958. The results of these surveys suggested that red sediments from the North-west Argentinian provinces of Salta and Jujuy were suitable for more detailed palaeomagnetic in- vestigations [ 1 ]. During a field expedition in 1969, 130 hand samples of Cambrian, Ordovician and Lower Devonian sediments were collected. The samples were orientated by use of both magnetic and sun compas- ses [2]. The palaeomagnetic results from the new col- lection are discussed. They show that the south palaeo- magnetic pole lay further to the north-east of South America in the Cambrian and Ordovician than pre- viously suggested. The South American results fall into a consistent pattern with results from other Gondwanan continents and form a single polar wan- der curve. This path is contrasted with the paths from Europe, North America and Asia and is compared with the geological records of the Palaeozoic mountain belts. 2. The sediments vary considerably but are frequently quartzitic, medium grained sandstones of a pinkish or light colour. An alternative explanation of the Lower Palaeozoic European palaeomagnetic results is that favoured by Briden [17] which involves an ex- cursion of the pole from a quasi-static position in the mid-Ordovician to mid-Silurian, and return to its for- mer position in the mid-Silurian to early Devonian, combined with some remagnetization of European Lower Palaeozoic results. I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. So after the Silurian Period the south palaeo- magnetic pole returned eastwards passing close to its Cambrian and Ordovician positions. This preferred explanation, of course, implies that remagnetization has not been as extensive as envisaged by Creer. North American Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results are scarce and a sensible polar wander path is difficult to construct. Creer again champions an ex- planation of the results in terms of remagnetization. This interpretation has been debated in the literature

An alternative explanation of the Lower Palaeozoic European palaeomagnetic results is that favoured by Briden [17] which involves an ex- cursion of the pole from a quasi-static position in the mid-Ordovician to mid-Silurian, and return to its for- mer position in the mid-Silurian to early Devonian, combined with some remagnetization of European Lower Palaeozoic results. I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. So after the Silurian Period the south palaeo- magnetic pole returned eastwards passing close to its Cambrian and Ordovician positions. This preferred explanation, of course, implies that remagnetization has not been as extensive as envisaged by Creer. North American Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results are scarce and a sensible polar wander path is difficult to construct. Creer again champions an ex- planation of the results in terms of remagnetization. This interpretation has been debated in the literature

d agreement with the geo- logical ideas outlined above on the age and origin of the Hercynian and Uralian mountain chains. The polar wander paths of the blocks associated with these oro- genies can be seen to converge by the Carboniferous. The separation of land masses across the ocean now represented by the Hercynian and Appalachian moun- tain belts was about 60 ° of arc (greater than the size of the present Atlantic) in the Cambrian Period. The palaeomagnetic results, however, do not fit in with the geological knowledge of the history of the Caledonian mountain chain [21 ]. The most noticeable problems are that (i) there is no hairpin bend in the North Ameri- can record, corresponding to that in the European and (ii) the Ordovician and Cambrian pole positions for the two blocks lie very close to each other. Neither of these suggests the "proto Atlantic" closed during the Silurian to form the Caledonian mountain chain. Further Lower Palaeozoic results from North America are needed before these apparent contradictions can be explained. Acknowledgements I wish to thank Professor K.M. Introduction Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic collections from South America were made in 1956 and 1958. The results of these surveys suggested that red sediments from the North-west Argentinian provinces of Salta and Jujuy were suitable for more detailed palaeomagnetic in- vestigations [ 1 ]. During a field expedition in 1969, 130 hand samples of Cambrian, Ordovician and Lower Devonian sediments were collected. The samples were orientated by use of both magnetic and sun compas- ses [2]. The palaeomagnetic results from the new col- lection are discussed. They show that the south palaeo- magnetic pole lay further to the north-east of South America in the Cambrian and Ordovician than pre- viously suggested. The South American results fall into a consistent pattern with results from other Gondwanan continents and form a single polar wan- der curve. This path is contrasted with the paths from Europe, North America and Asia and is compared with the geological records of the Palaeozoic mountain belts. 2. Introduction Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic collections from South America were made in 1956 and 1958. The results of these surveys suggested that red sediments from the North-west Argentinian provinces of Salta and Jujuy were suitable for more detailed palaeomagnetic in- vestigations [ 1 ]. During a field expedition in 1969, 130 hand samples of Cambrian, Ordovician and Lower Devonian sediments were collected. The samples were orientated by use of both magnetic and sun compas- ses [2]. The palaeomagnetic results from the new col- lection are discussed. They show that the south palaeo- magnetic pole lay further to the north-east of South America in the Cambrian and Ordovician than pre- viously suggested. An alternative explanation of the Lower Palaeozoic European palaeomagnetic results is that favoured by Briden [17] which involves an ex- cursion of the pole from a quasi-static position in the mid-Ordovician to mid-Silurian, and return to its for- mer position in the mid-Silurian to early Devonian, combined with some remagnetization of European Lower Palaeozoic results. I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. So after the Silurian Period the south palaeo- magnetic pole returned eastwards passing close to its Cambrian and Ordovician positions. This preferred explanation, of course, implies that remagnetization has not been as extensive as envisaged by Creer. North American Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results are scarce and a sensible polar wander path is difficult to construct. Creer again champions an ex- planation of the results in terms of remagnetization. This interpretation has been debated in the literature

d agreement with the geo- logical ideas outlined above on the age and origin of the Hercynian and Uralian mountain chains. The polar wander paths of the blocks associated with these oro- genies can be seen to converge by the Carboniferous. The separation of land masses across the ocean now represented by the Hercynian and Appalachian moun- tain belts was about 60 ° of arc (greater than the size of the present Atlantic) in the Cambrian Period. The palaeomagnetic results, however, do not fit in with the geological knowledge of the history of the Caledonian mountain chain [21 ]. The most noticeable problems are that (i) there is no hairpin bend in the North Ameri- can record, corresponding to that in the European and (ii) the Ordovician and Cambrian pole positions for the two blocks lie very close to each other. Neither of these suggests the "proto Atlantic" closed during the Silurian to form the Caledonian mountain chain. Further Lower Palaeozoic results from North America are needed before these apparent contradictions can be explained. Acknowledgements I wish to thank Professor K.M. Laboratory techniques All the hand samples were returned to Newcastle upon Tyne where, whenever possible, three 2.5 cm diameter cores were drilled from each sample. One 2.5 cm high cylinder was then cut from each of the cores. Measurements of the magnetic remanence were made on a PAR spinner magnetometer or the No. 1 sensitive astatic magnetometer [2]. Step thermal cleaning of pilot specimens was carried out to deter- mine if weak secondary magnetizations could be re- moved by thermal partial demagnetization [2]. After each step of cleaning the initial susceptibility of the specimens was measured to determine whether chemi- cal changes had occurred during the thermal treatment. Fisherian statistics [5] have been used for the calcu- lation of mean directions and their errors, and unless stated otherwise all results have been corrected for the orientation of the bedding. 2.3. the Gondwanan curve with the North American, European and Asian Palaeozoic polar wander paths is discussed in terms of the welding of Pangaea. 1. Introduction Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic collections from South America were made in 1956 and 1958. The results of these surveys suggested that red sediments from the North-west Argentinian provinces of Salta and Jujuy were suitable for more detailed palaeomagnetic in- vestigations [ 1 ]. During a field expedition in 1969, 130 hand samples of Cambrian, Ordovician and Lower Devonian sediments were collected. The samples were orientated by use of both magnetic and sun compas- ses [2]. The palaeomagnetic results from the new col- lection are discussed. They show that the south palaeo- magnetic pole lay further to the north-east of South America in the Cambrian and Ordovician than pre- viously suggested. The South American results fall into a consistent pattern with results from other Gondwanan continents and form a single polar wan- der curve. This path is contrasted with the paths from Europe, North America and Asia and is compared with the geological records of the Palaeozoic mountain belts. 2. South American palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results 2.1. Geology The Lower Palaeozoic rocks are commonly exposed on large, structurally simple, north-south trending blocks or folds (figs. 1 and 2). The Cambrian sedi- ments lie unconformably on weakly metamorphosed Precambrian, with a basal conglomerate commonly developed. The sediments vary considerably but are frequently quartzitic, medium grained sandstones of a pinkish or light colour. They are assigned to the Cambrian Period simply on their stratigraphical level below Lower Tremadocian faunas, and on the occur- rence of inarticulate brachiopods and Skolithos tubes [3]. An alternative explanation of the Lower Palaeozoic European palaeomagnetic results is that favoured by Briden [17] which involves an ex- cursion of the pole from a quasi-static position in the mid-Ordovician to mid-Silurian, and return to its for- mer position in the mid-Silurian to early Devonian, combined with some remagnetization of European Lower Palaeozoic results. I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. So after the Silurian Period the south palaeo- magnetic pole returned eastwards passing close to its Cambrian and Ordovician positions. This preferred explanation, of course, implies that remagnetization has not been as extensive as envisaged by Creer. North American Lower Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic results are scarce and a sensible polar wander path is difficult to construct. Creer again champions an ex- planation of the results in terms of remagnetization. This interpretation has been debated in the literature

I prefer a similar explanation to that of Briden, in that the European polar wander path has followed a course in the direction of his ex- cursions, but that it turned around a sharp hairpin bend in the Silurian Period, and that the rate of move- ment of the pole did not vary as much as envisaged by Briden. Introduction Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic collections from South America were made in 1956 and 1958. The results of these surveys suggested that red sediments from the North-west Argentinian provinces of Salta and Jujuy were suitable for more detailed palaeomagnetic in- vestigations [ 1 ]. During a field expedition in 1969, 130 hand samples of Cambrian, Ordovician and Lower Devonian sediments were collected. The samples were orientated by use of both magnetic and sun compas- ses [2]. The palaeomagnetic results from the new col- lection are discussed. They show that the south palaeo- magnetic pole lay further to the north-east of South America in the Cambrian and Ordovician than pre- viously suggested. The South American results fall into a consistent pattern with results from other Gondwanan continents and form a single polar wan- der curve. This path is contrasted with the paths from Europe, North America and Asia and is compared with the geological records of the Palaeozoic mountain belts. 2. ly. 1. Introduction Volcanism in the Colli Euganei in Northern Italy, south of Padova, is characterized by two eruptive cycles. The first cycle was dated as Lutetian and Pria- bonian, which lies in the middle and upper Eocene (50-45 m.a.) according to stratigraphic methods [1]. For specimens mainly of the second cycle radiometric age determinations (K/Ar) by Borsi et al. [2] are avail- able yielding a middle to upper Oligocene age (32 m.a.). This age has been confirmed for one volcanic unit of the second cycle by stratigraphic investigations of Dieni and Decima [1 ]. In the earlier palaeomagnetic work by De Boer and Schouten [3] samples of the second eruptive cycle were presumed to have an age between upper Miocene and upper Pliocene, which is 15-5 m.a. All these age determinations suggest an age of 50 45 m.a. for the first eruptive cycle and an age of roughly 33-10 m.a. for the second and more active eruptive cycle, which might have reached its climax in lower Miocene (25 m.a.). All contain abundant quartz and feldspar (predominantly plagioclase) and varying amounts of clinopyroxene, orthopyroxene, biotite, apatite and opaques. Hornblende occurs in sections from sites 11, 12, 14, 17 and 18, generally mantling clinopyroxene. Specimens from sites 11, 12, 14, 15, 17, 18 and 21 contain iddingsite, probably as an alteration product of iron-rich divine. The amount and proportions of the dark minerals vary so widely that no percentages can be given as typical. The range is from about 30% mafics at site 1 to about 3% at site 15. Potassium feldspar, when it occurs, is micro- cline, usually in perthite. Under the ore microscope the opaques are seen to be magnetite and ilmenite, which often occur together in single grains. The prevalence of plagioclase over K-feldspar, the ubiquity of biotite and the common predominance of clinopyroxene over orthopyroxene make it ques- tionable whether these rocks can be regarded as true charnockites. They are referred to here as charnock- itic rocks. The geology of the Mirnyy Station area and the complexity of these charnockitic rocks is described in detail by Ravich et al. [8]. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: he Fen palaeo- magnetic pole position depends on the question whether the magnetization is primary and reflects the Lower Cambrian geomagnetic field direction or whether it is secondary. Therefore the possibility of thermal as well as chemical remagnetization has to be considered. A thermal event of any importance after the em- placement of the Fen rock complex would likely reset the K-Ar biotite ages of the Fen rocks. However, ac- cording to Priem et al. [6], such rejuvenations of the K-Ar ages are conspicuously absent. It is therefore im- plausible that the magnetization of the r~dberg is secon- dary as a consequence of thermal remagnetization. Essential to the question of whether the NRM is pri- mary or has been acquired by chemical remagnetiza- tion, is the origin of the hematite in the r6dberg. As has been discussed already, the bulk of the hematite is considered to have been primarily deposited. Although some magnetite is present in the rCdberg, showing al- teration into hematite, the textural features of the he- matite do not indicate that this process took place on an important scale. Considering the hematite as a pri- mary mineral, the NRM of the ri~dberg may be con- sidered to be primary as well and not to be due to che- mical remagnetization. From a geological point of view there are no indica- tions for remagnetization of the rCdberg. Hence, we may consider the NRM as having been acquired during the origin of the r~dberg. The direction of the stable mag- netization was determined after a.f. demagnetization at 500 Oe peak value. Introduction The Paganzo Basin lies on the continental side of the Andes in north-west Argentina (fig. 1). Palaeomag- netic studies in the area were first carried out by Creer in 1958 [1]. Following this work more detailed collec- tions, particularly of Middle Paganzo sediments, were made in 1967 by Embleton [2, 3]. These rocks were subjected to thermal demagnetization and were shown to be highly suitable for palaeomagnetic investi- gation. In 1969 and 1970, further collections were made at new localities in order to give a more com- plete palaeomagnetic record for the interval of time covered by Paganzo sedimentation. K-Ar and palaeomagnetic results from an investi- gation of a basalt in the sequence have been presented previously, Thompson and Mitchell [4]. The palaeo- magnetic results from the sandstone collections are presented below and compared with results from oth- er continents. 2. Geology Deposition of sediments in the Paganzo Basin be- gan after the Acadian-Breton phase of the Carbonifer- ous Geosyncline to the west of the Basin [5]. During the early period of deposition material was provided by local sources, and depressions in the Basin were al- most completely filled with conglomerates and coarse sandstones. Marine intercalations are found in the Lower Paganzo sequences, but correlation is still diffi- cult between local centres. Middle Paganzo sediments are similar throughout the Basin, consisting typically of cross-bedded siltstones and fine-grained red sand- stones, commonly with a calcareous cement; the total thickness of sediments is around 1500 m. Basaltic flows and ash bands are found at several horizons. Sediments of the Upper section are again more varied, due to renewed tectonic movements in both the source areas and in the Basin itself. The palaeo- magnetic results from the sandstone collections are presented below and compared with results from oth- er continents. 2. Geology Deposition of sediments in the Paganzo Basin be- gan after the Acadian-Breton phase of the Carbonifer- ous Geosyncline to the west of the Basin [5]. During the early period of deposition material was provided by local sources, and depressions in the Basin were al- most completely filled with conglomerates and coarse sandstones. Marine intercalations are found in the Lower Paganzo sequences, but correlation is still diffi- cult between local centres. Middle Paganzo sediments are similar throughout the Basin, consisting typically of cross-bedded siltstones and fine-grained red sand- stones, commonly with a calcareous cement; the total thickness of sediments is around 1500 m. Basaltic flows and ash bands are found at several horizons. Sediments of the Upper section are again more varied, due to renewed tectonic movements in both the source areas and in the Basin itself. Geology Deposition of sediments in the Paganzo Basin be- gan after the Acadian-Breton phase of the Carbonifer- ous Geosyncline to the west of the Basin [5]. During the early period of deposition material was provided by local sources, and depressions in the Basin were al- most completely filled with conglomerates and coarse sandstones. Marine intercalations are found in the Lower Paganzo sequences, but correlation is still diffi- cult between local centres. Middle Paganzo sediments are similar throughout the Basin, consisting typically of cross-bedded siltstones and fine-grained red sand- stones, commonly with a calcareous cement; the total thickness of sediments is around 1500 m. Basaltic flows and ash bands are found at several horizons. Sediments of the Upper section are again more varied, due to renewed tectonic movements in both the source areas and in the Basin itself. Geology Deposition of sediments in the Paganzo Basin be- gan after the Acadian-Breton phase of the Carbonifer- ous Geosyncline to the west of the Basin [5]. During the early period of deposition material was provided by local sources, and depressions in the Basin were al- most completely filled with conglomerates and coarse sandstones. Marine intercalations are found in the Lower Paganzo sequences, but correlation is still diffi- cult between local centres. Middle Paganzo sediments are similar throughout the Basin, consisting typically of cross-bedded siltstones and fine-grained red sand- stones, commonly with a calcareous cement; the total thickness of sediments is around 1500 m. Basaltic flows and ash bands are found at several horizons. Sediments of the Upper section are again more varied, due to renewed tectonic movements in both the source areas and in the Basin itself. The palaeo- magnetic results from the sandstone collections are presented below and compared with results from oth- er continents. 2. Geology Deposition of sediments in the Paganzo Basin be- gan after the Acadian-Breton phase of the Carbonifer- ous Geosyncline to the west of the Basin [5]. During the early period of deposition material was provided by local sources, and depressions in the Basin were al- most completely filled with conglomerates and coarse sandstones. Marine intercalations are found in the Lower Paganzo sequences, but correlation is still diffi- cult between local centres. Middle Paganzo sediments are similar throughout the Basin, consisting typically of cross-bedded siltstones and fine-grained red sand- stones, commonly with a calcareous cement; the total thickness of sediments is around 1500 m. Basaltic flows and ash bands are found at several horizons. Sediments of the Upper section are again more varied, due to renewed tectonic movements in both the source areas and in the Basin itself. All flows are normally mag- netized, and attempts to obtain radiometric ages for these flows were unsuc- cessful, and paleointensity determinations by the 'Thellier method' were un- reliable. The mean virtual geomagnetic pole, (880N, 1100W) is not signifi- cantly different from the rotation axis, suggesting that the lavas erupted over a period that spans at least several thousand years. The between-site angular dispersion SB, is used as a measure of the secular variation. SB=6.00 with respect to the mean VGP, and SB=6.20 with respect to the axis of rotation with a 95 percent confidence interval for the latter of 5.20<SB<7.80. Potassium-argon dating indicates that the minimum time between eruptions of individual but genetically related ash-flow cooling units is on the order of 0.8 m.y. As this interval is long in comparison with the secular variation of the direction of the geo- magnetic field, in a given volcanic province the direction of natural thermoremanent magnet- ization is a unique characteristic of each cooling unit. Ash-flow sheets investigated include the Stone Cabin Formation, the tuff of Pancake Summit, the Windous Butte Formation, the Needles Range Formation, the Bates Mountain Tuff, and the tuff of Clipper Gap, of Oliogcene to early Miocene age. The original areas of individual ash-flow cooling units are as great as 8,000 km 2; the volumes, 1,300 km 3. The paleomagnetic correlations, made over distances up to 200 km, confirm most of the previously made lithologic correlations and allow more accurate delineation of single cooling units. This swarm probably resulted as the consequence of initial rifting between Greenland and Labrador, and a reversal of magnetisation has been found which is correlated on the basis of K—Ar age determinations (~-168 m.y.) with the Mateke event of the Middle Jurassic (Bajocian). All of fifteen sites show significant grouping of directions after a.f. cleaning; three have anomalous directions of magnetisation while the remainder (nine normal, three reversed) give a combined mean direction of D 336°, 1 66° (095 = 4.6°) with a palaeomagnetie pole at 191°E, 72° N. The dykes exhibit the same corelation between polarity and deuteric oxidation state as that found in Tertiary volcanics. There is a systematic change in magnetisation across the dyke swarm in south Greenland from normal to anomalous, to reversed directions; this is interpreted as due to lateral migration of the response to the regional stress field with time. The pole position lies in the vicinity of Jurassic poles from North America after closing the Labrador Sea according to the reconstruction of Bullard, Everett and Smith, but the scatter of these latter poles precludes a confirmation of this reconstruction for Middle Jurassic and earlier times. 1. Sixteen flows ranging in elevation from 900 to 2680 ft. showed normal magnetization with upward inclination, consistent with the position of India in the southern hemisphere during the period of their eruption. Four flows from elevation 450 ft. to 730 ft. showed intermediate as well as discor- dant directions. The paleomagnetic results obtained from these flows have been correlated with those of Deccan traps from other areas. The amount of paleosecular variation represented by these flows has been estimated and compared with that from similar vertical sequences of traps studied from other areas. It has been found that the magnitude of paleosecular variation varied during the period of Deccan trap activity. An estimate of continental drift has been made from mean pole position of the several vertical sequences of traps. Based on petrologic and K-Ar radiometric age studies, Richards and White (1970) have subdivided the batholith as mapped by Cairnes (1944) into three complexes . They restrict the term "Chilliwack batholith" to a complex of three plutons (not sampled in the present study) straddling the Canada - U.S. A. border around Chilliwack Lake where Daly (1912) originally d e fin ed the unit. Five K -Ar determinations from this com ­ plex give upper Oligocene to lower Miocen e age of 26 to 2 9 m. y. The other two units are the Hope and Mount Barr plutonic complexes (Fi g. 1-1). The Hope plutonic complex outcrops a few miles southeast of Hope, B. C . It is composed of a central pluton of leucocratic quartz monzonite giv ­ ing an age of 41 ± 2 m. y . (R ichards and White, 19

which give an age of 35 ± 2 m. y. The complex is therefore considered to be upper Eocene to lower Oligocene in age. The Mount Barr plutonic complex is centred around Wahleach Lake between the Chilliwack and Hope complexes . The main pluton has a quartz monzonite core grading radially outwards to quartz diorite. Within the core th ere is a younger stock of biotite hornblende granodiorite and a still younger stock of leu cocratic biotite quart z monzonite. An offshoot granophyric dyke is the fourth pluton includ e d in the complex. The K-Ar radiometric ages reported by Richards and White (1970) of 21 ± 1, 18 + 1, and 16 ± 1, by Baadsgaard et~ . Whillans ABSTRACT The magnetization of a rock sample is measured by moving a sample from the centre of one detection coil to that of another, the coils being co-axial. The field acting on the specimen can be varied between 0 and 1000 oersteds and the temperature of the specimen can be varied between 20 ° C and 700 ° C. Furthermore, the remanent magnetization acquired during crystallization of magnetic materials can be investigated using the required compounds in an oxidizing or reducing environment. Results obtained with this instrument for a 25% magnetite (Fe304), 75% Alundum Cement mixture show the dependence of the coercive force, the intensity of the isothermal magnetization and the thermal remanent magnetization on the grains ize of the magnetite which .spanned discrete intervals in the range of 2µ.m to 1600µ.m in the experiments. Symons ABSTRACT The Hope and Mount Barr felsic plutonic complexes outcrop in the Cascade Mountains in southernmost British Columbia. Intrusive rocks of sialic composition have rarely been studied paleomagnetically because of remanence instability, however, a stable primary remanent magnetization has been isolated in 5 of 7 sites from eac h complex after alternating field demagnetization . Individual plutons within each complex give coherent clusters of either normal or reversed remanence directions indicating that they were intruded and coo l ed sequentially rather than concurrently. The upper Eocene to lower Oligocene Hope complex gives a p ol e position of 15l.9°W, 87.7°N (om 6.1°, l\p 5,1°) which is concordant with poles from coeval North American units. The mid-Miocene Mount Barr pole position of 85.8°W, 72.4°N (om 14.6°, op 13 .3°) is slightly discordant possibly because of non-representative sampling. The results suggest that these comp lex es have not been rotated relative to the North American craton since their emplacement. The H ope and Mount Barr plutonic complexes were sampled during the summer of 1969 as part of an extensive paleomagnetic study of felsic plu­ tons in th e Canadian Cor dill era . They we r e sampled as representativ e of the youngest, least tectonically disturbed and unmetamorph osed felsic plutons known (M c Taggart and Thompson, 1967). By comparing their remanence dir ec tions with those obtained fr om contemporaneous units known to have stable r emanent magnetization, they provide a test to determine whether fel ­ sic plutons can yield reliable paleomagnetic data. Relativ e ly few paleomag­ netic studies hav e been carried out on rocks of this composition and only some of these indicate the retention of a stable primary remanence (Hays and Scharon, 1966; Gramme et al. , 1967; Symons, 197la and 197lb;Spall, 1971). Other studies have involved felsic rocks that were remagnetized during meta­ morphism (Spall, l 970a) or possess unstable remanence only (Spall, l 970b; Yaskawa et al., 1 966 ). Based on petrologic and K-Ar radiometric age studies, Richards and White (1970) have subdivided the batholith as mapped by Cairnes (1944) into three complexes . They restrict the term "Chilliwack batholith" to a complex of three plutons (not sampled in the present study) straddling the Canada - U.S. A. border around Chilliwack Lake where Daly (1912) originally d e fin ed the unit. Five K -Ar determinations from this com ­ plex give upper Oligocene to lower Miocen e age of 26 to 2 9 m. y. The other two units are the Hope and Mount Barr plutonic complexes (Fi g. 1-1). The Hope plutonic complex outcrops a few miles southeast of Hope, B. C . It is composed of a central pluton of leucocratic quartz monzonite giv ­ ing an age of 41 ± 2 m. y . (R ichards and White, 19

which give an age of 35 ± 2 m. y. The complex is therefore considered to be upper Eocene to lower Oligocene in age. The Mount Barr plutonic complex is centred around Wahleach Lake between the Chilliwack and Hope complexes . The main pluton has a quartz monzonite core grading radially outwards to quartz diorite. Within the core th ere is a younger stock of biotite hornblende granodiorite and a still younger stock of leu cocratic biotite quart z monzonite. An offshoot granophyric dyke is the fourth pluton includ e d in the complex. The K-Ar radiometric ages reported by Richards and White (1970) of 21 ± 1, 18 + 1, and 16 ± 1, by Baadsgaard et~ . (1961) of 18 and 18 m.y. indicat e a mid-Miocene age for the complex . Whillans ABSTRACT The magnetization of a rock sample is measured by moving a sample from the centre of one detection coil to that of another, the coils being co-axial. The field acting on the specimen can be varied between 0 and 1000 oersteds and the temperature of the specimen can be varied between 20 ° C and 700 ° C. Furthermore, the remanent magnetization acquired during crystallization of magnetic materials can be investigated using the required compounds in an oxidizing or reducing environment. Results obtained with this instrument for a 25% magnetite (Fe304), 75% Alundum Cement mixture show the dependence of the coercive force, the intensity of the isothermal magnetization and the thermal remanent magnetization on the grains ize of the magnetite which .spanned discrete intervals in the range of 2µ.m to 1600µ.m in the experiments. Symons ABSTRACT The Hope and Mount Barr felsic plutonic complexes outcrop in the Cascade Mountains in southernmost British Columbia. Intrusive rocks of sialic composition have rarely been studied paleomagnetically because of remanence instability, however, a stable primary remanent magnetization has been isolated in 5 of 7 sites from eac h complex after alternating field demagnetization . Individual plutons within each complex give coherent clusters of either normal or reversed remanence directions indicating that they were intruded and coo l ed sequentially rather than concurrently. The upper Eocene to lower Oligocene Hope complex gives a p ol e position of 15l.9°W, 87.7°N (om 6.1°, l\p 5,1°) which is concordant with poles from coeval North American units. The mid-Miocene Mount Barr pole position of 85.8°W, 72.4°N (om 14.6°, op 13 .3°) is slightly discordant possibly because of non-representative sampling. The results suggest that these comp lex es have not been rotated relative to the North American craton since their emplacement. SUMMARY There are strong arguments to believe that the Hope and Mount Barr felsic plutonic complexes retain a stable primary remanent magnetization that has been successfully isolated in this study. First, neither the cores nor plutons show petrologic evidence of metamorphic events that could produce a stable secondary remanent magnetization. Second, the remanence intensity d ecay curves and direction paths on AF step d emagne tization show that soft secondary remanence components aligned parallel to the earth 's present mag­ netic field are removed by the 100 or 200 oersted step . Fifth, remanence directions of the two complexes are well - grou p ed and sta­ tistically independent. After AF demagneti­ zation a stable remanent magnetization (RMs) was isolated for 17 sites. This RMs is thought to be primary for several reasons including the presence of truly reversed directions and the within-phase and within-pluton clustering of remanence directions. Next the diorite differentiated to concentrate a residual gabbroic magma which cooled in zones within the diorite. Simultaneously, syenitic and perthositic pegmatite was diff e rentiating from the monzonite and cooling to form the core of the stock. Giving each normalized site mean remanence direction unit weight, the sec ­ tion mean declinations (Dx), etc., were calculated (Appendix, Table 3). The resulting section mean directions for the six sections composed of five or more flows are shown on Figure 3b. None of the sections are obviously anomalous or obviously correlative except perhaps the Clinton Chasm and Hanceville sections . Further, the small values obtained for a:95 and lixe indicate that each of the six sections was likely deposited during one polarity interval. The specimens have been classified into three groups, based on their stability of natural remanent magnetism, using the alternating field demagnetization technique. Opaque petrological studies showed that the specimens which possessed magnetite- ilmenite exsolution were magnetically very stable. The specimens without any exsolution possessed weak and unstable magnetization. Sphene was identified in the alteration product of ilmenite using X-ray techniques. The remanence direc- tions of these samples were analysed to prove that the diabase acquired its remanence after the formation of the Kerr Lake Arch and the North Lorrain Basin structures. In 1971, Symons sampled 19 sites (sills and dikes) of the same rock in the Blind River-Elliot Lake area of Ontario. From the results of paleo- magnetic studies of the diabase, he tentatively concluded that the sheets and dikes of this area contained generally weak but stable pri- mary remanence components which tend to be masked by much stronger unstable components. He also concluded that the sheets were em- placed and cooled during several polarity in- tervals of the earth's- magnetic field about 2155 m.y. ago. These correlations, and the study by Steiner and Helsley (1972) dealing with the Kayenta, suggest the Chinle in the Colorado Plateau is not younger than the Newark Group but is somewhat older. The Redonda Member oi the Chinle Formation is almost certainly older than the upper two iormations ol the Glen Canyon Group. This means one cannot explain the observed polarity differences between the Chinle in eastern New Mexico and the Newark Group by saying the section sampled in this study is younger than the Newark. Likewise, paleontology rules out extremely rapid deposition of either the Chinle Formation or the Newark Group. The latter explanation is improbable when carried to the extent of assigning the Chinle a Middle Triassic age as proposed by McElhinny and Burek (1971). Until the temporal relation between the Chinle and Newark is clarified, the Newark group should not be used to define a reversal chronology.
